events.excerpt: Hey Cosmonauts, I’ve been exploring an idea for a privacy-focused Cosmos SDK chain and wanted to bring it here before going too far into implementation. The idea is called VeilRoute — a sovereign Cosmos blockchain that acts as a confidential settlement and asset-routing layer between IBC-connected chains. The problem I’m interested in is relatively simple: Cosmos has interoperability through IBC, but what if applications could route assets through a common privacy layer without publicly exposing every internal transfer, amount, balance, or ownership relationship? I’m not proposing changes to the Cosmos Hub or requesting governance funding. This is an early architectural discussion to get technical feedback from people working on Cosmos SDK, IBC, ZK systems, and interchain security. 1. The idea Imagine a user moving ATOM from Cosmos Hub to Osmosis. Today, the public source and destination transactions are observable, along with the relevant IBC packet information. With VeilRoute, the proposed flow would be: Cosmos Hub / Other IBC Chain | IBC Deposit | v +---------------+ | VeilRoute | | | | Shielded Pool | | ZK Validation | | Private Notes | | Audit Records | +---------------+ | IBC Withdrawal | v Destination IBC Chain Users would deposit an IBC asset, shield it into a private not
events.headline: [Discussion] VeilRoute: An IBC-Native Confidential Routing Chain with Threshold-Governed Disclosure

events.excerpt: Should the Cosmos Hub have its own price oracle? CosmWasm is now permissionless on the Hub, but there is no price oracle available to contracts. Pyth dropped CosmWasm, SEDA is EVM-only, and Band over IBC is slow and costs fees on every query. Without prices, we can’t build any advanced defi on the Hub. So these apps get built on chains like Injective or dYdX, and ATOM ends up used everywhere except on its own chain. Idea: integrate an enshrined oracle based on the Slinky fork. Validators would publish prices at every block, secured by the Hub’s own validator set, with no dependency on an external provider. And beyond the Hub: these prices could be distributed over IBC to any connected chain that lacks an oracle. The Hub would become an interchain’s price provider, with fees flowing back to ATOM stakers. Longer term: prices are only the first step. The same validator-voted mechanism could later carry other data the interchain needs, such as LST exchange rates, proof of reserves or other verified off-chain data. The Hub would become the interchain’s trusted data layer. The Community Pool could fund the development and audit. Would you support this direction? Validators, would you be willing to run an oracle sidecar? 20 posts - 7 participants Read full topic
events.headline: Oracle on Cosmos Hub

events.excerpt: v2.10.3 is a security and stability release on top of v2.10.2 . It's the public release of v2.10.3-priv , which most validators and major RPC providers already run. No hardfork, no database schema change, no resync required. Nodes can be upgraded one at a time, in any order. Highlights Execution : parallel (BlockSTM V2) balance reads are resolved correctly across a self-destruct boundary ( #2403 ). Shared block caches are size-capped and per-tx code hashes memoized, which lowers importer memory under heavy keccak / ecrecover load. Log counting while tracing no longer copies logs ( #2460 ). Txpool : pending chains stranded behind a head that can't be mined are evicted after txpool.strandedlifetime . Filtered addresses also apply to SetCode (type 4) authorizations. The pool signer is no longer swapped when allow-unprotected-txs is set ( #2464 ). Storage trie preload : segmented BFS queue for the preload, plus optional address-cache persistence across restarts. On a mainnet sentry, preload on restart drops from about 1h25m to about 4s. P2P : static peers stay dialed across jails and full dynamic slots ( #2438 ), and are kept out of the peer dropper. RPC : the execution slot is re-acquired between batch items, and the RPC execution pool request timeout from config is applied. Heimdal

events.excerpt: Why we’re posting. Proposals that put DAO money into liquidity pools often quote the pool’s fee rate (APR). We want to show, with real numbers, why that rate on its own can’t tell you whether the pool made money, and to suggest three simple questions anyone can ask when they see one. This isn’t about any particular proposal, and nobody paid for it. The short version. A pool’s fee rate only counts the money coming in. It leaves out what you lose when prices move. In our data, that loss took back all of the fees on Ethereum-style chains, and about half of them on Solana. What the fee rate leaves out When you put two tokens into a pool, you earn trading fees. That part is real, and it’s what the fee rate shows. But when one token’s price falls, the pool automatically ends up holding more of that token. So compared with simply keeping your two tokens in a wallet, you lose some money. The fee rate never shows this loss. It can’t go below zero. So we measured both parts together on real pool history: fees earned, minus the loss from price moves , compared with just holding the two tokens. 1. Same period, two very different results. Both rows cover January 2025 to July 2026. Each pool counts equally. pools fees loss from price moves what was left Ethereum-style chains (Ethereum, BSC, Ba
events.headline: Before you trust a pools fee rate (APR): what real pool history shows

events.excerpt: What's Changed Highlights Faster compilation and diagnostics. A series of optimizations across parsing, semantic analysis and lowering: module discovery (including plugin expansion) is now warmed up in parallel, the red-tree arena is built in place and chunked per item, trait-solving lookup contexts and code-size estimation are memoized, calls that would be inlined are no longer specialized first, and hash containers use foldhash. Diagnostics on large Starknet projects improved by up to ~40%. See Optimizations below. Build-independent Sierra output. The function chosen to carry the withdraw_gas check in a recursive cycle, and the order of impl candidates and impl type bounds, are now determined by a structural order instead of salsa internal ids, so the same program always compiles to the same Sierra regardless of parallel warmup. #10437 #10436 Rustc-style names for generated functions. events.excerpt: A 21-property attempt combining Certora Prover, Halmos, Foundry, mutation discrimination, historical regression testing, and deployed-bytecode binding. A special thanks to Certora, Halmos, and Foundry for making these tools available. And thank you to pegaslint and the agentic Closed_Models that made it possible. We performed an independent property_driven assurance campaign against Diamond PAU, including formal verification where tractable , symbolic and concrete production-path analysis, deployed_runtime binding, targeted mutation discrimination, and replay of five (5) historical regression classes. No live Diamond PAU vulnerability was established within the tested scope. Several properties remain explicitly unresolved because the formal models were not trustworthy or tractable enough to support stronger claims. This work is not : a claim that Diamond PAU is vulnerability-free; a universal formal verification of the system; a substitute for future review after code or configuration changes. Public assurance repository: pegaslint/diamond-pau-formal-assurance Why we did this Following the many high_profile exploits across crypto, we were inspired by the words of NEAR co-founder Ilia Polosukhin who believes formal verification can be an important part of reducing vulnerability ri

events.excerpt: [CONSTITUTIONAL] AIP: Update Arbitrum One and Nova L1-Pricing Parameters for Ethereum Glamsterdam Abstract This proposal updates the parentGasFloorPerToken and perBatchGasCharge parameters on Arbitrum One and Arbitrum Nova in response to Ethereum’s Glamsterdam upgrade. Glamsterdam changes the Ethereum gas costs associated with posting Arbitrum chain batches. Without corresponding parameter updates, the L1 fee paid by Arbitrum One and Nova users may no longer accurately reflect the cost of posting batches to Ethereum. The proposal authorizes targeted updates to the live parameters through the ArbOwner precompile. It does not introduce an ArbOS software upgrade or change the underlying L1-pricing algorithm. Motivation Arbitrum’s L1-pricing system estimates Ethereum gas cost of each batch, then uses that estimate to set the L1 fee paid by Arbitrum users and the amount the batch poster is paid back. Two parameters feed into this estimate: parentGasFloorPerToken , which mirrors Ethereum’s minimum gas charge for calldata; and perBatchGasCharge , which represents a fixed component of the estimated Ethereum gas cost attributed to each batch. The existing values reflect Ethereum’s pre-Glamsterdam cost structure. Following Glamsterdam’s activation, they may no longer accurately account for

events.excerpt: Since the DVP upgrade, ArbitrumDAO’s quorum is set as a share of delegated voting power: 50% for constitutional and 40% for non-constitutional proposals. This stopped token unlocks from pushing quorum up, but it moved the problem rather than solving it. Every delegated ARB that never votes now raises quorum without adding turnout, so incentives that reward delegation without checking whether that voting power is actually used can make quorum harder to reach. ABSTAIN votes count toward quorum and can carry thin proposals over the line, a large holder can delegate and stay silent to stall decisions, and lowering quorum again would make attacks cheaper. One possible answer is a neutral participation pool. The DAO funds it per epoch in advance, never per proposal, so nobody can buy turnout for their own vote. It pays only for votes actually cast: the same for FOR and AGAINST, less for ABSTAIN, with a cap per address. Rewards are computed from onchain VoteCast events and published as a Merkle root, so voters keep using Tally as usual. Delegates: is turnout still a real constraint after the DVP upgrade, and would a direction-neutral pool feel legitimate to you? In my free time I study consensus mechanisms and DAO governance. I’d build this as open source and may later apply for a grant
events.headline: Rewarding votes, not delegation: participation incentives under DVP quorum

events.excerpt: Building Trisara (Colosseum hackathon): session-aware pricing infra for RWA markets: a real clock for equity prices onchain. The BONER/HIMS case is the exhibit: one meme cornered ~42% of HIMS on-chain float and pushed the wrapped token to $132 against a $28 real close over a weekend with the NYSE closed. No arb window fast enough to hold the two together. Uniswap routes >99% of tracked stock-token DeFi deposits on Robinhood Chain, so this lands on your pools first. I verified the root cause live (Chainlink equity feeds frozen 37.7h over weekends). Trisara’s PoolTwapAdapter + GuardedSwapRouter collars flow when the reference market is closed: a plug-in, not a fork. Is session-aware pricing something v4 hooks on RH Chain should standardize?
